sentences.text:
Before
 Hon'Ble Shri Justice B. P. Sharma

On The 6 th Of October, 2025
 Criminal Appeal No. 810 of 1998
 Laxmichand (C.O. Dt. 08/09/2025 Abated) And Others
 Versus
 The State Of M.P.
 Appearance:
 Shri Prince Kumar Tripathi - Proxy counsel for appella
 Shri S.P. Chadhar - Government Advocate for respondent
 Shri Jagtendra Pd.Bansal - Advocate for the respondent
 Order

This criminal appeal has been preferred under Section 374(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973, assailing the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 23.03.1998 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, District Balaghat in S.T. No.122/94 whereby appellants No.2 & 3 were held guilty for the offence punishable under Section 376(2)(g) of IPC and sentenced to undergo R.I. for 10 years each with a fine of Rs.50/- each and appellant No.4 was held guilty for the offence punishable under Section 506-B of IPC with a fine of Rs.200/- with default stipulations.
2.
The appellant No.1-Laxmichand and appellant No.4-Chimanlal died during pendency of the appeal.
Therefore, this appeal stands abated so far as appellants No.1 & 4 are concerned.
3. At the outset, learned counsel for the appellants submit that he is not challenging the conviction part of the judgment.
He is only challenging sentence part of judgment.
It was argued that the statement of the victim is not corroborated NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:50133 2 CRA-810-1998 by the medical report.
The appellants have remained in the jail for more than 01 year.

4. During the pendency of this appeal, learned counsel for the appellant as well as for the complainant/prosecutrix submitted joint application, seeking permission to compound the offence on the ground that the parties have amicably settled their dispute.
By order dated 08.09.2025, the Registrar (J-II) of this Court was directed to record the statements of the parties with respect to the compromise.

Laxmichand (C.O. Dt. 08/09/2025 ... vs The State Of M.P. on 6 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/158851264/
1 5.
Pursuant thereto, the Registrar (J-II) recorded the statements of both parties on 25.09.2025 and verified the correctness and genuineness of the compromise.

In the report it has also been mentioned that prosecutrix voluntarily entered into the compromise with the appellant/accused with free will and volition and without any threat, coercion, or inducement and the complainant had expressed the non- willingness to proceed further in the case.

6. Counsel for the appellants submit that so far as the sentence awarded by the trial Court under Sections 376(2)(g) of the IPC is concerned, the appellants have already undergone jail sentence of more than 01 year.
The statement of the victim is not corroborated by the medical report.

Moreover,
compromise has already been entered into between the parties, therefore, while maintaining the conviction under Sections 376(2)(g) of the IPC the jail sentence may be reduced to the period already undergone by the appellants.

7. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.
8.

Though learned counsel for the appellants has not assailed the findings of conviction on merits and has confined his submissions only to the question of sentence on the basis of the compromise application, this Court is nonetheless under a legal obligation to scrutinize the correctness and sanctity of the conviction recorded by the trial Court.
On this aspect, I have carefully perused the judgment NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:50133 3 CRA-810-1998 of the trial Court and the evidence adduced during trial.
The trial Court, while appreciating the entire evidence in its proper perspective, has arrived at a well- reasoned finding of guilt against the appellants.

Upon independent reappraisal, I find that the conclusion so recorded by the trial Court is based on cogent reasoning and does not suffer from any perversity or illegality warranting interference by this Court.
Accordingly, the findings of conviction of the trial Court against the appellants as regards offence punishable under Sections 376(2)(g) of the IPC
is hereby affirmed.
9. Turning to the point of compromise, it is also significant to note that the compromise has been filed at the stage of appeal before this Court.

On this aspect, it would be relevant to note the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ishwar Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh [AIR 2009 SC 675], wherein the Apex Court has observed as under:
"15.

entities.text: Ishwar Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh [AIR 2009 SC 675]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In our considered opinion, it would not be appropriate to order compounding of an offence not compoundable under the code ignoring and keeping aside statutory provisions.

In our judgment, however, limited submission of the learned counsel for the appellant deserves consideration that while imposing substantive sentence, the factum of compromise between the parties is indeed a relevant circumstances which,
the Court may keep in mind."

10. On this point, the view of Hon'ble Apex Court in the Unnikrishnan alias Unnikuttan versus State of Kerala reported in AIR 2017 Supreme Court 1745 is also worth referring in the context of this case as under:-

2 "10.

In series of decisions i.e. Bharath Singh vs. State of M.P. and Ors., 1990 (Supp)
SCC 62, Ramlal vs. State of J & K, (1999) 2 SCC 213, Puttaswamy vs. State of Karnataka and Anr, (2009) 1 SCC 71 1, this Court allowed the parties to compound the offence even though the offence is a non-compoundable depending on the facts and circumstances of each case.

SCC 62

sentences.text: In some cases this Court while imposing the fine amount reduced the sentence to the period already undergone.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:50133 4 CRA-810-1998 11.

What emerges from the above is that even if an offence is not compoundable within the scope of Section 320 of Code of Criminal Procedure the Court may, in view of the compromise arrive at between the parties, reduce the sentence imposed while maintaining the conviction"
11.

In the case of Murali vs. State (2021) 1 SCC 726 , the Apex Court has held that the fact of amicable settlement/compromise between the parties can be a relevant factor for the purpose of reduction in quantum of sentence of convicts even in serious non-compoundable offences.
12. In the present case, it is seen that the parties have compromised the matter, which has been duly verified.

It is true that the offence under Sections 376(2)(g) of the IPC is not compoundable under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973,
therefore, the application for compromise cannot be allowed.

However, as held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in aforementioned case laws, in exceptional circumstances,
considering the voluntary settlement between the parties, the Court may give effect to such compromise at the stage of final disposal of appeal and further that where parties have amicably resolved their disputes and the complainant has unequivocally supported the compromise, the Court may, in the interest of justice and to maintain social harmony, modify the relief suitably by reducing the substantive sentence.

13. Considering the fact that the parties have entered into compromise, as also the period of incarceration already undergone by the appellants which is more than 01 year, I am of the considered opinion that the ends of justice would be met, if the sentence of imprisonment awarded by the trial Court is reduced to the period already undergone by appellants.
14. In the result, the conviction of the appellants under Sections 376(2)(g) of the IPC as recorded by the trial Court, is hereby affirmed.
However, the substantive NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-JBP:50133 5 CRA-810-1998 sentence of appellants is modified and reduced to the period already undergone by them.
The appellants are on bail.
The bail bond furnished by the appellants shall stand discharged.
15. This criminal appeal stands disposed of to the extent indicated hereinabove.
